disclaimer.normal_residence: Exchange almost always requires that you were normally resident in the issuing country when (and often while) you held the licence, and that you are resident in the destination when you exchange. EU law defines normal residence as living in a place for at least 185 days in each calendar year (Directive 2006/126/EC Art. 12). Several national authorities (e.g. Netherlands RDW) restate the same 185-day rule for non-EU licences. A licence obtained without meeting that condition is often void in the destination.
disclaimer.scope: Lawful exchange conditions only. This is not a guide to licence tourism, and the one-licence rule means there is no stacking to be done: you end up holding exactly one, from where you reside.
disclaimer.coverage: Seeded destinations (11): Germany, Great Britain, Netherlands, Ireland, France, Spain, Austria, New Zealand, Australia, Denmark, Portugal. EU/EEA mutual recognition is not expanded as third-country annex rows. Sub-national variance is flagged for US/CA/AU where instruments are state/province-level.
disclaimer.what_a_licence_evidences: A driving licence is best read as a RESIDENCE ARTEFACT, not a collectible. Under Directive 2006/126/EC the three rules lock together: issuance requires normal residence in the issuing state (art. 7(1)(e)); "No person may hold more than one driving licence" and a state "shall refuse to issue a licence where it establishes that the applicant already holds" one, verifying with other Member States through the EU driving licence network (art. 7(5)(a)-(d)); and on exchange the original is surrendered and the swap is recorded on the new licence (art. 11(6)). So the licence you hold is single, exclusive and anchored to where you actually live, which is why in practice it is widely accepted as evidence of address. That exclusivity is the point of this layer, not a limitation of it: the exchange network shows which residence histories convert into which documents.

agreements.name: EU/EEA — mutual recognition of driving licences
agreements.instrument: Directive 2006/126/EC art. 2(1); extended to the EEA EFTA states by EEA Joint Committee Decision No 29/2008 (Annex XIII point 24f)
agreements.basis: Art. 2(1): "Driving licences issued by Member States shall be mutually recognised." Quote-checked 2026-08-09 against the EUR-Lex text. Scope is the EU-27 plus Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway = 30. Switzerland is NOT covered: it is not a party to the EEA Agreement (art. 126(1) lists only the three EFTA states, and art. 128 still records Switzerland as a state that may apply), so Swiss licences travel on national third-country law — Germany places Switzerland in Anlage 11 to FeV s.31, the list of states OUTSIDE the EEA. The UK is likewise a third country since the transition ended on 31 December 2020.
agreements.exchange_article: Art. 11(1): a holder who has taken up normal residence in another Member State "may request that his driving licence be exchanged for an equivalent licence". Exchange is a right to REQUEST, not automatic, and is a separate article from the art. 2(1) recognition right.
agreements.residence_condition: Art. 12: normal residence means where a person usually lives "at least 185 days in each calendar year". It gates issuance (art. 7(1)(e)) and triggers the exchange right, and art. 7(5)(a) bars holding more than one licence.
agreements.third_country_carve_out: Art. 11(6) is the provision that forecloses licence laundering. Where a Member State exchanges a THIRD-COUNTRY licence for a Community model, the exchange "shall be recorded on the Community model driving licence", the original "has been surrendered", and if the holder then moves to another Member State "the latter need not apply the principle of mutual recognition set out in Article 2". So a non-EEA licence swapped in one member state does not reliably become EEA-wide.
agreements.superseded_note: Directive (EU) 2025/2205 repeals 2006/126/EC with effect from 26 November 2029; mutual recognition moves to its art. 3(6) and the residence test becomes a rolling "185 days of the previous 365 days" (art. 20(1)) rather than a calendar-year test.
agreements.exclusivity: Art. 7(5)(a): "No person may hold more than one driving licence". Art. 7(5)(b): a Member State "shall refuse to issue a licence where it establishes that the applicant already holds a driving licence", and art. 7(5)(c)-(d) require verification with other Member States via the EU driving licence network. Exclusivity is enforced and cross-checked, not merely asserted.

agreements.name: Netherlands — RDW
agreements.instrument: Regeling omwisseling niet-Nederlandse rijbewijzen art. 1 (country list), made under Reglement rijbewijzen art. 46(5)
agreements.basis: CORRECTION: our record described this as "countries outside EU/EFTA WITH AGREEMENT". There is no negotiated arrangement anywhere in the chain. Art. 1 reads "Voor omwisseling tegen een Nederlands rijbewijs komen in aanmerking de door de hierna [genoemde landen]" — a list the Netherlands designates. The word Overeenkomst in the Reglement refers to the EEA Agreement, never to a bilateral deal with an issuing state. Art. 2 is more unilateral still: RDW may exchange any foreign licence "om redenen, aan het algemeen belang ontleend" (for reasons of general interest), a discretionary domestic power with no counterparty.

agreements.name: Ireland — NDLS / RSA
agreements.instrument: Negotiated bilateral agreement/MoU, given domestic effect by Road Traffic Act 1961 s. 23A and the Road Traffic (Recognition of Foreign Driving Licences) Order 2007 (S.I. 527/2007), Schedule
agreements.basis: Genuinely two-layered, and forcing one label would lose the point. SUBSTANTIVELY bilateral: Ireland negotiates a reciprocal MoU, and the Department states agreements "may be made only when the authorities in each jurisdiction have studied and compared the licensing regimes". FORMALLY unilateral: s. 23A gives the Minister an order-making power and S.I. 527/2007 simply declares licences from "a state mentioned in the Schedule" recognised for exchange, so Ireland could delist without the counterparty. Recorded as bilateral_agreement because that is what creates the entry; the unilateral instrument is the delivery mechanism, not the deal.

agreements.name: Denmark — Danish Road Traffic Authority
agreements.instrument: BEK nr 203 af 04/03/2016 om ombytning af udenlandsk kørekort til dansk kørekort uden kontrollerende køreprøve, §§ 1-3
agreements.basis: The sharpest case for why kind matters. It LOOKS bilateral because the counterparty initiates: "Deltagelse i ordningen sker på baggrund af en ansøgning fra det pågældende land/delstat" — participation happens on the basis of an application FROM the country concerned. But no agreement is concluded; Færdselsstyrelsen decides alone and § 3 stk. 2 makes the decision unappealable to any other administrative authority. Initiation by a counterparty is not reciprocity. CORRECTION: our instrument string said "Group 1 / Group 2", conflating two different things — in BEK 550/2026 those are VEHICLE-category groups for medical fitness, while the country grouping is the separate § 1 and § 2 tracks of BEK 203/2016, labelled gruppe 1-/gruppe 2-lande on the agency site only.
